items.lede: On September 8, Omnis Pleasants filed its Schedules of Assets and Liabilities and Statements of Financial Affairs — two separate docket entries, Dkts. 254 and 255 — completing a submission that had been extended by court order (Dkt. 194) from the standard deadline.
items.body_md:
On September 8, Omnis Pleasants filed its Schedules of Assets and Liabilities and Statements of Financial Affairs — two separate docket entries, Dkts. 254 and 255 — completing a submission that had been extended by court order (Dkt. 194) from the standard deadline. The schedules are substantive-and-important: they constitute the debtor's sworn itemization of the estate's assets, liabilities, executory contracts, and creditor claims, and they establish the factual baseline against which every plan treatment, claim objection, and sale valuation argument will be measured. For creditors, the schedules are the first official picture of what the estate actually holds and owes under oath — including where the debtor's own accounting lands relative to WVEDA's $50-plus-million claim, the TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC secured positions, and the broad field of unsecured creditors. Any material divergence between the schedules and the petition's estimated ranges ($50–$100 million in assets; $50–$100 million in liabilities) or between the schedules and proofs of claim as they come in will shape the claim-objection and lien-priority fights that sit beneath the sale process. The full text of Dkts. 254–255 has not been pulled into this record, so the specific line-item figures and any anomalies will require a PACER pull to assess with precision.

Today, September 9, the debtor filed Dkt. 256, the agenda of matters scheduled for hearing — a procedural filing keyed to an upcoming court date. Given that the October 13 omnibus hearing (Dkt. 253) is the next docketed court event, the agenda most likely relates to that date, though the filing's text has not been pulled for this record and the precise matters listed cannot be confirmed without a PACER review. Agenda letters are ordinarily procedural and routine, but in this case the October 13 hearing carries substantive freight: the HSF Kramer retention (still unresolved, with a further revised proposed order at Dkt. 246 but no final approval), the final cash-collateral order (estate still operating under interim authority, Dkt. 50), and whatever bidding-procedures and sale-timeline matters Judge Owens carried over from September 3.

The schedules filing is the most consequential docket movement since the September 3 hearing. It opens the 30-day window under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 within which the U.S. Trustee and parties in interest can scrutinize the debtor's disclosures, and it gives Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants — both of whom are challenging the bona fides of this filing — sworn estate data to test against their dismissal arguments. The dismissal motion hearing remains on track for November 3. October 13 is the next concrete milestone.

items.lede: On September 9, the Poolin docket recorded a Certification of No Objection at Dkt. 208, paired with supplemental declarations at Dkts. 206 and 207 filed the day prior — together, these resolve the contested posture of the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors' retention application for Pachulski Stang Ziehl & Jones LLP.
items.body_md:
On September 9, the Poolin docket recorded a Certification of No Objection at Dkt. 208, paired with supplemental declarations at Dkts. 206 and 207 filed the day prior — together, these resolve the contested posture of the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors' retention application for Pachulski Stang Ziehl & Jones LLP. Dkts. 206 and 207 are supplemental declarations — one from Committee Chair and one from Bradford J. Sandler of PSZJ — filed in further support of the retention application (Dkt. 179) that the U.S. Trustee had been given an extended deadline to oppose. The Certification of No Objection at Dkt. 208 signals that no timely objection was lodged, and the retention of PSZJ as UCC counsel, effective August 13, 2026, should now be ripe for entry of an approving order by Judge O'Hagan. The practical consequence is that the Committee has cleared the last procedural hurdle to full engagement of its restructuring counsel — a meaningful step given that PSZJ's mandate includes scrutinizing the § 363 sale process, evaluating any transfers subject to avoidance, and pressing the recovery position of the approximately 11,700 IOU wallet holders against a $163.7 million unsecured claim pool. These docket entries are classified substantive (professional retention contested by the U.S. Trustee touches estate governance and Committee capacity) but routine as a matter of outcome — the supplemental declarations addressed whatever disclosure gap prompted the extension, and no objection materialized.

The Committee's parallel retention application for M3 Advisory Partners, LP as financial advisor (Dkt. 201, filed September 4) carries an objection deadline of September 11. No certification of no objection has yet issued on that application; if M3 clears that deadline without opposition, the Committee will have both restructuring counsel and financial advisory capacity in place before the sale hearing. That sequencing matters: the Committee is the principal counterweight to the Debtors on sale economics, and an equipped Committee entering the September 18 sale hearing is structurally different from one still awaiting professional retention approvals. The trustee motion, with a hearing set for October 21, remains the structural overhang on the entire process and is unaffected by these filings.


The auction of the West Texas mining assets — the Pyote and Tarbush sites — is scheduled for tomorrow, September 10,
 assuming qualified bids were submitted by the September 8 deadline. No secondary source has confirmed whether competing bids were received or whether the auction will proceed as a live competitive event rather than a walkover for stalking-horse Thor CALAP LLC and its $52 million floor offer; the docket is the only authoritative source on that question. 
The sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan in Trenton is set for September 18 at 11:00 a.m. Eastern,
 with 
September 16 as the final deadline for creditors to file sale objections.
 The next concrete milestone is tomorrow's auction call — the first hard data point on whether any bidder exceeded the $52 million stalking-horse floor and what, if anything, the competitive process returned above it.

Lee entered Dkt. 485 — an order that simultaneously terminated one or more pending motions, per the docket's "Order AND ~Util - Terminate Motions" designation. The order followed a Response filed yesterday, Dkt. 484, which itself arrived after the opposition at Dkt. 483 (filed August 25).
items.body_md:
On September 9, Judge Eumi K. Lee entered Dkt. 485 — an order that simultaneously terminated one or more pending motions, per the docket's "Order AND ~Util - Terminate Motions" designation. The order followed a Response filed yesterday, Dkt. 484, which itself arrived after the opposition at Dkt. 483 (filed August 25). That sequencing — opposition, then a further response, then an order closing motions the same day — is consistent with the court resolving a fully briefed administrative motion on the papers. The most plausible candidate remains Google's August 21 Administrative Motion to Consider Whether Cases Should Be Related (Dkt. 478), which drew an opposition on its August 25 deadline (Dkt. 483) and now a reply-level response (Dkt. 484) before today's order.

The case-relation motion matters because a grant would link this proceeding — or a related action — to a coordinated docket under a single judicial assignment, with downstream consequences for discovery scheduling, briefing calendars, and the pace at which class certification issues get resolved. A denial keeps each proceeding on its own track. The "Terminate Motions" utility event confirms the court has formally closed at least one motion, but the identity of every motion terminated, the direction of the ruling, and any conditions attached cannot be stated from the docket text alone; the full text of Dkt. 485 on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 is the controlling document and the priority pull. Until it is retrieved, the outcome is unverified and is not stated here.

The longer-standing open item — the content and effect of the August 24 omnibus order at Dkt. 482, which resolved class certification, the sanctions motion, and the intervention motion — remains unreported by any secondary outlet as of this briefing. That document continues to control whether the class is certified, in what form, and whether the Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix intervenors (Dkt. 468) are in the case. The next concrete milestone is the full text of Dkt. 485, which should be pulled immediately; if today's order granted the case-relation motion, any resulting judicial reassignment or coordination order would follow and should be treated as the next reportable event.

items.lede: On September 8, Oriel Bachar filed a sealed letter (Dkt. 95) designated as related to Dkt. 93 — Skillz's own sealed letter filed September 4 within 48 hours of Judge Walrath's September 2 compel order (Dkt. 92). The content of both letters remains off the public record.
items.body_md:
On September 8, Oriel Bachar filed a sealed letter (Dkt. 95) designated as related to Dkt. 93 — Skillz's own sealed letter filed September 4 within 48 hours of Judge Walrath's September 2 compel order (Dkt. 92). The content of both letters remains off the public record. Dkt. 94 — a Notice of Service filed September 7 with an attached service list — is procedural and carries no independent substantive weight. The unnumbered entry filed September 8 alongside Dkt. 95 mirrors the pattern of the unnumbered entry filed alongside Dkt. 93 on September 4: in both instances, a sealed letter was accompanied by an unassigned, unconfirmed counterpart entry on the docket.

The sealed exchange between the parties is the operative development to track. Skillz filed Dkt. 93 shortly after obtaining the partial compel order; Bachar has now replied under seal with Dkt. 95. That sequence — creditor files under seal, foreign representative responds under seal, both letters tethered to the same underlying compel order — suggests the parties are likely in correspondence with the court over the scope, timing, or compliance logistics of Dkt. 92's production and deposition directives, the specific terms of which have not appeared on the public docket and must be confirmed from the order text itself. The possibility that one or both letters addresses a compliance dispute, a request for a protective order over what is produced, or a timing accommodation cannot be ruled out; the sealed posture of both letters prevents a firmer read. If either letter triggers court action — an order, a scheduling entry, or a hearing notice — that filing will take the classification of whatever it resolves.

The controlling external variable remains the Israeli 45-day standstill on collection efforts that began August 3, 2026, placing its expiration on or around September 17 — eight days out, per __[FIRY investor release, investors.skillz.com](https://investors.skillz.com/news/news-details/2026/Israeli-Court-Says-Papaya-Gaming-Should-Improve-Its-Debt-Settlement-Proposal-to-Repay-730-Million-to-Skillz-a-FIRY-NYSE-FIRY-Company-and-Declines-to-Send-It-to-a-Creditor-Vote/default.aspx)__. No public reporting confirms whether Tel Aviv's Judge Lushi-Abudi has extended, modified, or allowed that standstill to run to its natural end, and no FIRY investor release or press wire has appeared since August 31 with an update. 
The Israeli court suggested during the August 26 hearing that managers and shareholders who received dividends might be required to contribute to the revised settlement — a signal that the revised plan may reach beyond Papaya's operating cash and into distributions already made.
 The arrangement manager, Attorney Gil Oren of Arnon, Tadmor-Levy, is the party responsible for driving a revised plan, and his work product — whenever it appears — is the critical variable for Skillz's recovery quantum.

The next concrete milestones are: the September 17 standstill expiration in Israel (and any court action preceding or following it); any unsealing or court response triggered by Dkts. 93 and 95; and public confirmation of the specific production and deposition deadlines imposed by Dkt. 92.

items.lede: On September 8, the Terraform Labs docket recorded a single Certificate of Mailing (Dkt. 1331) — ministerial filing infrastructure, no bearing on recovery or timing.
items.body_md:
On September 8, the Terraform Labs docket recorded a single Certificate of Mailing (Dkt. 1331) — ministerial filing infrastructure, no bearing on recovery or timing.

Today is accordingly a context day. The most directly relevant open variable for Class 5 recovery posture remains the SEC's distribution plan for the $123.1 million Fair Fund — funded by Tai Mo Shan's consent-order payment — for which an August 20 deadline to submit eligibility criteria and payment procedures was reported by __[CryptoSlate](https://cryptoslate.com/sec-faces-aug-20-deadline-to-unlock-123-million-recovery-fund-for-terra-investors/)__. No public confirmation that the SEC met that deadline or that the plan has been filed has appeared in the search results; until the agency publishes a distribution plan, that pool remains locked. Separately, the authorization motion filed August 19 (Dkt. 1321) still shows no corresponding order on the docket, leaving its scope and effect unresolved.

On the litigation side, the plan administrator's $4 billion suit against Jump Trading, William DiSomma, and Kanav Kariya in the Northern District of Illinois remains the single largest potential recovery catalyst for the estate. The protective-order dispute — Jump argued the May 1, 2026 amended complaint improperly drew on documents produced under the bankruptcy protective order, prompting Judge Lefkow to stay litigation deadlines and direct the administrator to seek clarification from the Delaware court — has not produced a public resolution since it was last reported. The investor securities class action in the Northern District of California (Judge Pitts), in which Jump's motion to dismiss was denied on September 3 per __[Law360](https://www.law360.com/classaction/articles/2521162)__, runs as a separate but parallel pressure vector; Jump now defends on two fronts simultaneously, which may concentrate settlement incentives on the administrator's suit. Secondary-market activity in the Class 5 pool — the $3,454,036.42 claim transferred to Serrur Investment Partners, LP (Dkt. 1312, executed July 27, filed August 3) being the most recent confirmed trade — continues to reflect market participants positioning ahead of any distribution event.

The next fixed milestone remains December 31, 2026, the court-extended wind-down deadline. Resolution of the protective-order dispute before Judge Shannon — which, once clarified, would re-open the stayed Illinois deadlines — is the most proximate gating event for the Jump litigation, and thus the most meaningful near-term determinant of recovery trajectory for Class 5 claimants.

items.body_md:
On September 4, JND Legal — the settlement administrator — distributed consolidated claim notices to all claimants in the Bartz class, triggering a 30-day contest window that is now running. 
Each notice summarizes the claimant's submitted works, identifies any other party that filed a claim for the same title, and discloses what percentage of the award each party has claimed; it also provides a unique Claim Number, PIN, and link to a secure review portal.
 
Most claimants face no dispute and are asked only to confirm the details; they may also update payment information and address if those have changed since the original claim was filed.
 
Disputed claims are those in which different claimants to a single work — typically an author and a publisher or co-author — have asserted competing percentage splits; when a claimant logs in, the portal shows what each party has claimed for that work.
 The 30-day response window controls the pace of the reconciliation phase and, by extension, the readiness of the distribution calculus ahead of the November 15 first-payment estimated deadline — making timely claimant action the operative variable between now and that date, per __[Authors Guild](https://authorsguild.org/news/important-information-regarding-anthropic-copyright-settlement-claim-notices/)__ and __[TAA](https://blog.taaonline.net/2026/09/next-steps-in-bartz-v-anthropic-settlement-resolving-claim-percentage-differences/)__.


Authors and publishers that have each filed claims for a given work in which the claimed percentages do not match are required to meet and confer with the other claimants for that work to attempt to agree on the split.
 
During that process, the claimants and the settlement administrator will look to the underlying publishing contracts governing the disputed work for guidance on how the payout should be allocated.
 The dispute-resolution layer adds an indeterminate amount of time to the reconciliation process for contested titles; the extent of that friction across the 440,490 claimed works will determine whether the administrator can certify a clean distribution file in time to hit the November 15 target. Nothing on the district docket reflects any court involvement in resolving those disputes at this stage — the meet-and-confer obligation runs between claimants and the administrator, not through Judge Martínez-Olguín.

The district docket itself has been static since Dkt. 689 (Hartnett withdrawal, September 3). No new filings have appeared. The two fee-only Ninth Circuit appeals — No. 26-5391 (Edelson PC / Oppenheim + Zebrak) and No. 26-5455 (Cowan DeBaets Abrahams & Sheppard LLP) — remain without briefing schedules, and objector Stacy Lynn Werner's Dkt. 687 remains in procedural limbo pending a conforming refiled notice. None of those appellate tracks affect the payment timeline or the reconciliation process now underway. The next concrete case milestone is Anthropic's $450 million Scheduled Payment 1, due September 25, 2026, which funds the first distribution tranche estimated at approximately $2,203.56 per work; the 30-day claimant-contest window that opened September 4 will close on or around October 4 — before that installment lands — making it the more immediate operational deadline for class members.

items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
